doc.title: Sonny Igoe interviewed by Monk Rowe, Emerson, New Jersey, July 31, 2003

chapter: Road life, race and Woody Herman/Tommy Dorsey
title: Leaving Woody Herman and being fired by Tommy Dorsey
summary: Igoe quits Herman for the baby, joins Dorsey, is fired, and gets paid via the union.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: story short, my wife got pregnant early and had to leave me on the road, she had to go home. So my father and mother found a place in North Bergen, they were building new apartments in those days and so we got an apartment over there. And when she had the baby I wanted to get time off because of the baby. And Woody wouldn’t give it to me. So I said well I’m going to have to leave the band. He says okay. So I left the band. And the last night I had with the band we were playing at Buckeye Lake, Ohio, it’s a big place where bands played. And across the lake was Tommy Dorsey’s band playing the same night. Now they got through an hour before we did so they came around to us in their bus to hear our band. So we were playing our last couple of sets and I knew Louie Bellson, he was with the band. And Louie came in. And so anyway we were playing our last couple of sets and Tommy’s talking to Woody and Woody told him that I was leaving. He says, “he’s leaving the band?” And he says, “how come?” He says, “well his wife’s going to have a baby.” “Oh where does he live?” “New Jersey.” He says, “well we’re going to be playing in New Jersey for a month.” So Louie Bellson was leaving. He didn’t have anybody set. So he had his manager come up and talk to me about joining his band. So I left Woody one day and joined Tommy Dorsey two days later at the Syracuse Hotel up in Syracuse. And so I was supposed to play at a place called the Rustic Cabin for a month with the band. Because we lived just a few miles down the pike so to speak, down the Palisades. So anyway he gets on the bandstand and says, “it’s great to have a” blah-blah- blah-blah. So anyway the last night we had a jam session and it was very good and a lot of fun and all that kind of stuff, on the stand in the hotel. And so we packed up all this stuff and all the stuff is going on a truck or a bus or however they got it around in those days, I forgot. So anyway I’m in bed about four and the phone rings. And I pick up the phone and he said, “Sonny?” I says, “yes.” He says, “this is so-and-so” I forget the guy’s name, the manager of the band. He said, “Tommy just told me to fire you.” And I said, “what?” I said, “I thought he said he liked the way I played.” He said, “I don’t know” he said, “get rid of that guy.” So I said, “okay.” But I said, “I want the money for the Rustic Cabin or I’m going to take it to the union.” So he said, “I’ll tell you what I’ll do. I’ll give you” — I forget what I was going to get for the — it was pretty good money for me at that time, I think it was about 300 bucks a week, but he said, “I’ll tell you what I’ll do, I’ll give you 400 dollars cash tomorrow and we’ll forget about it.” Because then he was going to put the rest in his pocket and he was going to tell Tommy he had to pay me and he could put the rest of that money in his pocket. He was famous for that. So that’s why some of those band leaders died broke you know, their managers were doing that to them. So anyway as it happened I went to the union and said this is what they said, this is what has happened and they said okay, we’ll back you. And I said, “but they want me to come there every night and just hang around for a while.” He said, “well how far is it from your © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

home?” I said, “six or eight miles.” He said, “well why don’t you keep it quiet, just go up there and hang around for an hour and leave.” And he said, “we’ll back you up and we’ll get your money.” And so they did, they got the money, they got the full 1200 bucks; 1200 bucks was 1200 bucks. And so they got the money for me. And so the first night I went up there Tommy was busy resetting the band, he didn’t like the way they had set it up. So my drums were on the corner. They had unloaded them. So I went over to get the drums and I said, “hey Tommy, I thought you said you liked the way I played.” And he had a very raspy kind of voice. He said, “listen to me, kid, I don’t want anybody in my band who I think is putting me on.” He said, “all you young guys think you play different from somebody else.” I said, “well I don’t think I’m any different but I thought you said you liked it.” He said, “nah I don’t want anybody in my band who I think is putting me on.” So then he says, “did you ever hear of Ray Wetzel?” I said, “sure, the great trumpet player.” He said, “he was on this band four times before I let him stay.” I said, “do me a favor, don’t call me four times.” But he called me twice.
He called me twice after that incident. So anyway I never worked with him again but that was it, I took my drums and went home. But that’s another little story over a couple of years.
